title: A walk-and-talk for hard decisions
description: Some decisions will not move while you sit still. Why walking side by side loosens stuck thinking — and how to run a walking conversation that ends with an answer.

body.heading: Why walking works on stuck minds
paragraphs: A decision you have circled for days at a desk often moves within ten minutes of walking. Part of it is the body: steady rhythm and changing scenery give the anxious, looping part of the mind something to do, and the problem-solving part gets room to work underneath.

Part of it is geometry. Walking side by side, looking ahead rather than at each other, makes hard things easier to say — it is why so many honest conversations happen in cars and on walks, and so few across a desk.

body.heading: Run the walk like a meeting
paragraphs: State the decision out loud in one sentence before you set off: 'By the end of this walk I want to know whether…' A vague walk produces vague relief; a named question produces an answer, or at least a sharper question.

Walk for at least twenty minutes before judging any idea — the first ten are usually the old arguments warming up. When a thought feels true, say it out loud; hearing your own voice commit to a sentence is information no amount of silent circling provides.

body.heading: Land the plane
paragraphs: On the final stretch, agree the smallest next step and its date — not the whole future, just the first move. Decisions feel heavy when they pretend to be final; most are really just next steps wearing a crown.
Write the step down when you get home, before the kettle boils. A decision that survives being written down was a real one.

takeaway: Name the decision in one sentence, walk twenty minutes before judging ideas, and finish with one small dated next step.
